planting.note: Plant bare-root crowns or container divisions in spring into rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil in shade to mostly shade.

directions: This Japanese species from Nagasaki Prefecture forms a flat mound of glossy, puckered green leaves that are shiny on the underside. In late summer into September it sends up tall, heavily branched, candelabra-like scapes bearing an unusually large number of dark lavender flowers arranged almost in whorls, making it one of the latest and showiest-blooming wild hosta species. Give it consistent moisture and rich, humusy soil in shade to mostly shade; it is reported to tolerate verticillium wilt better than many hosta relatives. Divide clumps in spring if increase is desired.

planting.note: Set container divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in light to deep shade; spreads gradually by rhizomes.

directions: Formally described in 2015, this Chinese evergreen Solomon's seal was recognized as a distinct species after long cultivation under a cultivar name; it is thought to have arisen naturally from Disporopsis pernyi and Disporopsis fuscopicta parentage. Upright, dark-green stems carry highly glossy, evergreen foliage, topped in mid-spring by small, star-shaped white flowers held close to the leaf axils. It tolerates light to deep shade and spreads slowly into an attractive year-round groundcover patch. Keep soil evenly moist and rich in organic matter for best foliage color.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained woodland soil in semi-shade; fast-growing and clump-forming once established.

directions: Native to Mount Emei in Sichuan, China, this evergreen relative of Solomon's seal has dark green foliage marked with distinctive snake-skin-like mottling on the stems. In early summer it produces pendulous, lemon-scented, pale greenish-yellow flowers that hang beneath the arching stems, larger than those of most related species. It is a fast-growing, clump-forming groundcover best sited beneath trees in semi-shade with regular moisture and well-drained, humus-rich soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into leafy, moist but well-drained soil in shade; stems emerge mottled lilac at the base.

directions: Collected from stony sites in broad-leaved evergreen forest on Mount Emei, Sichuan, this compact evergreen Solomon's seal has arching stems with distinctly wavy-margined, oblong-lanceolate leaves. Lightly fragrant, bell-shaped, cream flowers marked with dark reddish-purple and yellow-green spotting inside appear at the leaf axils in summer, followed by dark purplish berries. Its smaller stature compared to other Disporopsis species suits it to the front of a shaded woodland bed in leafy, evenly moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full to light shade; slow to establish but long-lived.

directions: Native from southern China into northern Vietnam, this evergreen rhizomatous perennial is one of the larger-growing members of the genus, slowly reaching up to a yard tall. Arching stems carry alternate, elliptic leaves, with nodding, bell-shaped flowers held in the leaf axils that are notably larger than those of related species. It is easily grown in moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full to light shade and is reliably hardy through most winters where sited.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into good, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, shady spot; overwinter indoors or under cover outside zone 9.

directions: Collected from the wet tropical mountains of northern Luzon in the Philippines, this evergreen Solomon's seal relative carries narrow, shiny leaves on slender stems. Off-white bell-shaped flowers speckled with green and brown hang beneath the foliage in late spring to early summer, followed by purple berries. Because it comes from a frost-free tropical habitat, it needs a sheltered, consistently shaded site with good, humus-rich soil and regular moisture, and is best grown as a container or conservatory plant outside the mildest frost-free zones.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
